young.html: T. S. Eliot was born in St. Louis, Missouri, and moved to England as a young man. After the terrible First World War, he wrote a long poem called The Waste Land about a world that felt broken, like a dry land waiting for rain.

The poem is built from many voices and pieces, like a collage: bits of old songs, Bible stories, Shakespeare, legends about knights searching for the Holy Grail, and people talking in London. It ends with the sound of thunder over a desert, as if rain might finally come.

young.cap: Pick a part of the poem and see the older books it borrows from.

young.html: A collage poem. Cut out ten interesting phrases from old magazines, newspapers or a page you print out. Arrange them on paper so they make a feeling or a little story. Glue them down and give your poem a title. That is a bit like how Eliot built The Waste Land.

full.html: Thomas Stearns Eliot (1888–1965) grew up in St. Louis, studied philosophy at Harvard, and settled in London in 1914, where he worked in a bank and later as a publisher. He became a British subject in 1927, the same year he was received into the Church of England, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948. The Waste Land appeared in 1922 in two magazines and then as a book in New York, with Eliot's own notes. His friend Ezra Pound cut the draft nearly in half, and Eliot dedicated the poem to him.
The poem's 433 lines are in five sections. It opens by turning spring, usually a time of joy, into a time of pain, because new life stirs up memories and longings:

full.text:
April is the cruellest month, breeding
Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing
Memory and desire, stirring
Dull roots with spring rain.
full.author: T. S. Eliot
full.work: The Waste Land, I. The Burial of the Dead, lines 1–4

full.html: The voices shift without warning: a woman remembering a childhood sledding trip, a fortune-teller with her cards, crowds of office workers crossing London Bridge like Dante's dead, a nervous couple, gossip in a pub, a sailor drowned at sea. Eliot's notes point to the legend of the Fisher King, whose wounded land stays barren until a knight asks the right question, which he took from Jessie Weston's book on the Grail stories and from Frazer's Golden Bough.

In the last section, "What the Thunder Said," travelers cross a dry, rocky land toward a chapel. Thunder speaks three words from an ancient Hindu text, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata, which Eliot's notes translate "Give, sympathise, control." Near the end the speaker says:

full.text: These fragments I have shored against my ruins
full.author: T. S. Eliot
full.work: The Waste Land, V. What the Thunder Said, line 430

full.name: gb-eliot-fragments
full.cap: The five sections and some of the sources Eliot names in his notes: our summary.

full.html: The poem's method is its meaning. A culture shattered by war is shown in fragments; the old stories are still there, broken, but perhaps able to be gathered up. Whether the rain comes is left open.

The Waste Land became the landmark of modernist poetry: no single speaker, no story told in order, quotations in several languages, and sudden shifts of tone. Readers then and now have argued whether that difficulty is necessary or a barrier.
Trying to understand every reference on first reading. Read it aloud, like music, and notice the moods; the notes can come later.

items: Dante's Inferno, earlier on this ladder, gives Eliot his image of crowds of the living who seem already dead.
Augustine's Confessions and the Buddha's Fire Sermon meet in Part III, "The Fire Sermon": two great teachers from East and West who warn against burning desires.
Shakespeare's Tempest echoes through the poem's drowned sailor and its hopes of a sea-change.
Frazer's Golden Bough, in this era's social science, gave Eliot the old myths of a dying and reviving land.
Eliot's later Four Quartets moves from the waste land toward faith.
Can old stories and words help rebuild a broken world?
Why might spring feel "cruel" to someone who has lost a great deal?
What do "give, sympathize, control" ask of a person?
Should a great poem be easy to understand?

questions: Why do you think Eliot called April "the cruellest month"?
The poem is made of many voices. Whose voice is easiest to hear?
What would "give, sympathize, control" look like in a family?
How might a whole country feel after a terrible war?
Do you like poems that are puzzles, or poems that are clear? Why?
care: Some passages describe unhappy adult relationships briefly and indirectly; the lesson does not quote them. Best for teens and adults.
